nameStory: The "saltmarsh" part of this plant's name tells you exactly where to find it - thriving in the salty, wet edges where ocean meets land. It's called a "false" foxglove because its tubular pink flowers look remarkably similar to true foxgloves, but it belongs to an entirely different plant family. Think of it as nature's imposter, wearing a foxglove costume while living a completely different lifestyle!
description: Saltmarsh false foxglove is a slender annual wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall in coastal salt marshes. It has a delicate, branching appearance with narrow leaves and produces small tubular pink or purple flowers that bloom from late summer into fall. This specialized plant has adapted to thrive in salty conditions that would kill most other flowering plants. You'll recognize it by its wispy, almost grass-like stems topped with cheerful trumpet-shaped blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular pink to purple flowers about half an inch long, with 5 rounded petal lobes that flare out from a narrow tube - they feel papery-thin and have a delicate, almost tissue-like texture

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, linear leaves that are opposite on the stem and feel slightly succulent or fleshy - they're adapted to store water and handle salt spray

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, much-branched plant that sways easily in coastal breezes, with a wispy appearance that might remind you of a delicate grass until you spot the flowers

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found in salt marshes or brackish areas - if you're not near the ocean or tidal areas, you're not looking at this species

habitat: Look for saltmarsh false foxglove exclusively in coastal salt marshes, brackish wetlands, and the upper edges of tidal areas throughout New England's coastline. It grows in the salty, periodically flooded soils that most plants can't tolerate, often alongside salt marsh asters, glasswort, and cordgrass. You'll find it from the rocky coasts of Maine down to Connecticut's tidal marshes.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with narrow leaves, barely noticeable among other marsh vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow taller and begin branching extensively, developing their characteristic wispy appearance but not yet flowering.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming time from August through October, when the distinctive pink tubular flowers make identification easy - this is the best time to spot and identify this species.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to survive the winter in the salt marsh soil.

funFact: This little wildflower is actually a "salt vampire" - it's what botanists call a halophyte, meaning it not only tolerates salt water but actually requires it to complete its life cycle, making it one of the few flowering plants that would die in your typical freshwater garden!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other false foxgloves, but remember the habitat rule: if it's not in a salt marsh, it's not saltmarsh false foxglove! Purple false foxglove grows in dry, inland areas and is much taller, while slender false foxglove prefers sandy but non-salty soils.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "foxglove," this plant is completely unrelated to the true foxgloves (Digitalis) that are famous for their heart medication compounds. The false foxgloves were moved from the snapdragon family to the broomrape family relatively recently as DNA studies revealed their true relationships.
compareHints: Saltmarsh false foxglove is the only member of its genus that requires salty conditions - this habitat preference makes it the easiest false foxglove to identify. While purple false foxglove is much taller and grows in dry uplands, and slender false foxglove prefers sandy but fresh soils, our saltmarsh species is smaller and exclusively coastal. The flowers are also typically smaller and more delicate than its inland relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple false foxglove is the most common and robust of the false foxgloves in New England, with larger flowers and broader leaves than slender false foxglove.
Among New England's false foxgloves, slender false foxglove has the thinnest, most thread-like leaves - much narrower than purple false foxglove's broader lance-shaped leaves.

Tenlobe false foxglove is distinguished from other New England false foxgloves primarily by its flower structure - it has ten corolla lobes versus five in most relatives, and tends to have more deeply divided, thread-like leaves than purple false foxglove.
Compared to its false foxglove relatives, Nova Scotia false foxglove is distinguished mainly by its coastal habitat requirement and very limited range.
Beach false foxglove differs from its relatives like purple false foxglove and slender false foxglove primarily by its coastal habitat and extremely narrow, thread-like leaves.
